cases.title: The Renaissance Wave

artifact.hint: The Mona Lisa vanished from the Louvre, and ACME now believes the thief is advancing through a handpicked list of Renaissance masterpieces.

pattern.label: Renaissance masterworks escalation
pattern.summary: The thief is moving from one flagship Renaissance work to the next, using chapel plans, museum inventories, and prestige routes to predict where ACME will arrive too late.

briefing.intro: Paris, late October 1953. The Mona Lisa — La Joconde in the museum's own ledgers — vanished from the Louvre overnight. It is the second time in the century the painting has gone missing, but this is no copycat. The Allied art-recovery programs wound down two years ago, leaving a tangle of unverified provenance papers across postwar Europe. Customs at every border still rubber-stamps half its paperwork from memory. Someone calling themselves The Cartographer is exploiting that chaos, moving works through the same smuggling corridors that hid Nazi loot in Altaussee. ACME picks up the file before the trail crosses the Channel — or worse, the Brenner.
briefing.namingTell: In Parisian paperwork the painting is always La Joconde; if a document calls her Mona Lisa, the document is not Parisian.

cases.solvedText: ACME reaches Rome in time and catches the thief during the Vatican strike. The Renaissance sequence collapses before the final masterpiece can be taken.

route.title: The Louvre breach
route.chapterSummary: October 1953. The Louvre's Salle des États is empty where La Joconde hung. The Service de Restitution des Œuvres d'Art is still cleaning up half a decade of postwar paperwork, and the dispatch room has lost a working day's records to water damage. Whatever the thief left behind is in the photos, the porter's chair, and a half-burned shipping ledger.
route.learningGoal: Identify which postwar rail corridor the trail follows out of Paris, and recognise that two more corridors remain unread.
route.thiefClaim: The Mona Lisa belongs back in Italy where she was painted, and the postwar paperwork can be made to agree.
route.truthComplication: Two of the three Italian shipments are decoys; one is the trail. The Cartographer is not returning La Joconde — they are using a return narrative as cover for a trafficking circuit.
route.escalationText: ACME has the Mona Lisa case before the Cartographer hands her off in Italy.
route.investigationPrompt: Read the breach scene. Find the porter, decode the only legible row of the ledger, and lock the next stop on the trail.

innerMonologue.text: Twelve years since Allied troops stopped this from being looted to Linz. Six since the last Vermeer crawled home from Altaussee. Now somebody walks La Joconde out the front door — Mona Lisa, if you're the kind of buyer who doesn't read French.
Three crates means three shipments. The thief used the Louvre's own paperwork. Audacious — and recent enough that the wax is still soft.
Red wax. The Modane tunnel runs to Turin, then Milan. Old smugglers' route — the maquis used it in '43.
One seal placed, two waiting. The other corridors are still legible somewhere on the line. Modane first. The rest of Italy after — and something the ledger doesn't list at all, after that.
The curator returns the call. With the porter's seals in hand the reading list stops being scholarship and starts being a route prediction.

customLocations.name: Dispatch Desk
customLocations.description: A half-burned dispatch ledger, three coloured wax seals visible on its routing column.

night-porter.intro: He hasn't moved from the porter's corridor. He'll talk — but only to questions, not to broad fishing.

questions.text: What time did your shift start?
questions.answer: Eight in the evening. La Joconde was on the wall when I clocked in. I made my rounds at nine and again at midnight. By two she was gone.

questions.text: Did you see anyone moving crates through dispatch?
questions.answer: Three crates. The dispatch desk usually only does two on a Friday. I didn't read the labels — but I saw the wax. Three colours.
One red, one green, one blue. The red one had a Modane railway tag clipped beneath the wax. I do not know what was in any of the crates — but the seals were not Louvre seals.

questions.text: Did you see who left the dispatch room?
questions.answer: A tall figure. Long coat. Empty hands — that was the strange thing. The crates moved without anyone visible carrying them. By the time I crossed the corridor the figure was gone and so was La Joconde.

artifact.hint: A Hokusai print and its maritime ledger vanished, leaving blue pigment traces and a shipping account.

pattern.label: Ukiyo-e print and maritime image route
pattern.summary: The thief follows Hokusai records, Dutch print-trade catalogues, and a final American collection ledger.

route.learningGoal: Connect Hokusai, Edo print culture, Mount Fuji imagery, and the print's Japanese context.
route.thiefClaim: The print's origin makes every later collection secondary.
route.truthComplication: The Great Wave is rooted in Japan but became globally influential through circulation.

route.learningGoal: Show how maritime trade routes and Dutch-Japanese contact opened channels through which Japanese prints could travel outward.
route.thiefClaim: The print left Japan through a single corrupt export corridor that can be reversed cleanly.
route.truthComplication: Trade routes moved objects and ideas, but they rarely form a simple reversible chain.

route.learningGoal: Show how print collecting and Dutch-Japanese cultural routes helped move Japanese images into Europe.
route.thiefClaim: European records are just contamination to be removed.
route.truthComplication: Collection routes can distort context, but they also explain how influence spread.

route.learningGoal: Trace how Japanese prints reshaped European taste, collecting, and modern art through Parisian salons and critics.
route.thiefClaim: Paris proves the image was consumed as fashion, not respected as culture.
route.truthComplication: European enthusiasm distorted context, but it also formed part of the print's modern worldwide significance.

route.learningGoal: Expose the thief's final attempt to turn a global collection history into a fake proof of improper removal.
route.thiefClaim: An American collection file proves the print wandered too far from its rightful home.
route.truthComplication: Global collecting can be unequal, but the final forged transfer still has to be disproved with evidence.

clues.title: Dejima note
clues.text: The missing ledger references a western Japanese harbor where Dutch trade paperwork once touched Japanese print routes. The margin says Nagasaki.

clues.title: Domestic westbound hop
clues.text: The first move stays inside Japan and heads west toward a port city rather than directly overseas.

clues.title: Port wrapping
clues.text: The wrapping includes harbor codes and cargo twine used by maritime traders, not by inland print sellers.

clues.title: Domestic customs stamp
clues.text: The first customs stamp is domestic and Japanese. The export stage starts later.

clues.title: Dutch print-trade entry
clues.text: The Nagasaki trade ledger points to Amsterdam and a Dutch old-master catalogue shelf that handled Japanese print records.

clues.title: Blue-paper shipment
clues.text: The wrapping included machinery paperwork and a packet marked for a canal-side print dealer.

clues.title: Westbound art freight
clues.text: The crate moved west from Tokyo to Europe, not across the Pacific. The routing label mentions a temperate maritime destination.

clues.title: Dutch customs stamp
clues.text: The customs stamp is Dutch, and the permit number matches a museum print department in Amsterdam.

clues.title: Paris salon card
clues.text: A Rijksmuseum circulation card points to Paris salons where Japanese prints changed European taste and criticism.

clues.title: Short continental hop
clues.text: The next move is a short west-southwest hop to a European capital on the Seine rather than across the Atlantic.

clues.title: Critics' index
clues.text: The critics' index is full of Paris addresses, collectors, and salon notes about Japanese prints.

clues.title: French collector seal
clues.text: The sealed packet matches a Paris collector's route rather than another Dutch museum transfer.

clues.title: Freer accession number
clues.text: The Paris correspondence contains a copied accession number for an Asian art collection in Washington, D.C., where the thief plans the final proof swap.

clues.title: Atlantic sleeve
clues.text: The next crate crossed the Atlantic toward a capital city, not a commercial art hub.

clues.title: Industrial cover manifest
clues.text: The cover manifest lists aircraft parts and electronics. It fits an American customs file better than another European stop.

clues.title: Washington catalogue
clues.text: The catalogue request names Washington, D.C. and an Asian art gallery. ACME marks the American collection ledger as the final proof point.

deadEnds.default: The print-trade ledger does not support this destination.
deadEnds.United Kingdom: The British Museum appears in print history, but this route's records move through Amsterdam first.
deadEnds.Japan: The theft begins in Japan. The ledger points outward after the first scene.

artifact.hint: The Sun Stone file was stolen from Mexico City, along with an excavation note and a cathedral-era storage reference.

pattern.label: Calendar stone and Mesoamerican provenance route
pattern.summary: The thief is not crossing borders first; the pattern hides the object inside Mexico City's own museum, temple, and excavation records.

route.learningGoal: Introduce the Sun Stone as a national museum object tied to Mexica identity and Mexico City.
route.thiefClaim: A national display still separates the stone from its sacred urban root.
route.truthComplication: The museum protects and interprets the object as part of modern national memory.

route.learningGoal: Connect the object to Tenochtitlan, Mexica sacred geography, and the archaeological center of the city.
route.thiefClaim: The temple site is the only context that matters.
route.truthComplication: The site is crucial, but the object's modern museum life is also part of its cultural biography.

route.learningGoal: Expose a false local transfer that turns valid site evidence into a forged custody claim.
route.thiefClaim: A nearby museum archive can make the local return official.
route.truthComplication: Even a local route needs proof; proximity cannot replace records.

clues.title: Temple site note
clues.text: The stolen object card names Mexica sculpture and a site-evidence file at Templo Mayor. The thief is still inside Mexico City.

clues.title: Mesoamerican bibliography
clues.text: The bibliography points to Aztec and Maya pyramids, a Mesoamerican provenance argument, and the old center of Tenochtitlan.

clues.title: Local cover manifest
clues.text: The manifest lists vehicles and electronics, but every address stays in Mexico City. There is no border-crossing customs mark.

clues.title: No export permit
clues.text: The registry confirms no legal export permit exists. The next scene is domestic and tied to the temple site.

clues.title: Museum case number
clues.text: The Templo Mayor site card matches a museum case number a few streets away. The false provenance will be filed at the Templo Mayor Museum.

clues.title: Curator's shortcut
clues.text: A visiting curator heard the courier ask for the shortest walk from the excavation site to the museum archive.

clues.title: Local warrant
clues.text: The warrant names Mexico City and the Templo Mayor Museum archive. The pattern is local, but the evidence is complete.

deadEnds.default: The Sun Stone evidence is unusually local; this lead does not support an international jump.
deadEnds.Spain: Colonial records may matter later, but the current excavation evidence stays in Mexico City.
deadEnds.Guatemala: Mesoamerican context is relevant, but the object and scene evidence both point to Mexico.
